CONTEXT. This page is the worked numerical example ('Als Beispiel') for the three-observation scheme set out on the previous page, folio 61. That scheme uses the constants Sigma, A, A', A'', B, B'' and the relation that ties the middle geocentric distance to 1/r'^3. The data fix the meaning of the notation:
- The angles labelled alpha, alpha', alpha'' are geocentric ecliptic longitudes of the body: 28°47'58.29", 13°46'22.16", 344°1'41.14".
- The log column beside them is log tan beta, i.e. theta = tan of the geocentric latitude: 9.7576714 = log tan 29°47', 9.4952314 = log tan 17°22', 9.5347649n = log tan(-18°53').
- The third column (235°13'41.00", 249°24'21.80", 256°18'36.05") gives V, V', V''. These behave as solar longitudes: log D = 9.99469, 9.99359, 9.99320 decrease the way the Earth-Sun distance does in Nov-Dec.
- So D, D', D'' are the solar distances R.
- The body moves about 45° retrograde and from +30° to -19° latitude while the Sun moves 21°. That suggests a very close-approaching object, plausibly the comet of Nov-Dec 1805 (Biela's comet). This is my conjecture.

(1) THE THREE SINES OF SOLAR-LONGITUDE DIFFERENCES.
- log sin(V''-V') = 9.0799240 (6°54'14").
- log sin(V''-V) = 9.5559441 (21°04'55").
- log sin(V'-V) = 9.3890511 (14°10'41").

(2) THE DETERMINANT Sigma = theta sin(alpha''-alpha') - theta' sin(alpha''-alpha) + theta'' sin(alpha'-alpha), as on folio 61.
- log sin(alpha''-alpha') = 9.6956013n.
- log sin(alpha''-alpha) = 9.8477455n.
- log sin(alpha'-alpha) = 9.4137509n.
- The three products are -0.28400869, +0.22030264 (after the minus sign) and +0.08872102.
- Hence Sigma = 0.02501497, log 8.3982597.
- A recomputation in the second column gives 0.02507359, log 8.3992165.
- After correcting the positions (see (5)) Gauss recomputes it at lower right: 0.22027345 + 0.08873227 - 0.28397783 = 0.02502789, log Sigma = 8.3984242. This is the value used on the next page.

(3) THE CONSTANTS A, A', A''. The definition is A^(i) = D^(i) [theta sin(V^(i)-alpha'') - theta'' sin(V^(i)-alpha)].
- Gauss tabulates log sin(V-alpha'') = 9.9761826n, sin(V'-alpha'') = 9.9985838n, sin(V''-alpha'') = 9.9996562n.
- He also tabulates sin(V-alpha) = 9.6484176n, sin(V'-alpha) = 9.8134756n, sin(V''-alpha) = 9.8676939n.
- The corrected block, column 1, runs as follows:
  - theta'' sin(V-alpha) = 9.1827581;
  - theta sin(V-alpha'') = 9.7338749n;
  - Gaussian addition log 0.1075879 = log(1 + 0.15228/0.54177);
  - the bracket is 9.8414628n (= -0.69405);
  - adding log D = 9.9946906 gives log A = 9.8361534n.
- In the same way log A' = 9.8930181 (sign as written) and log A'' = 9.9092884.
- The next row holds the interpolation weights (t''-t')/(t''-t) = 10^(9.5142895-10) = 0.3268 and (t'-t)/(t''-t) = 10^(9.8281405-10) = 0.6732. They sum to 1, the hypothesis k = k'' (k/k'' = 1) being made.
- Applying them: weighted A term = 9.3504429n, the A' term with weight 1 (log 0.0) = 9.8930181, weighted A'' term = 9.7374289.
- These are the pieces of formula 1/ on folio 61: Sigma delta' = A' + [(t'-t)k''A'' + (t''-t')kA]/[(t'-t)k'' + (t''-t')k] * {1 + M(V'-V)(V''-V')/(2r'^3)}.
- The upper-right block is the same computation with the uncorrected data. There 9.7562034n is evidently 9.9762034n.
- The 'Erste Hypothese k/k''=1, M=1' columns combine these into the coefficients of the form delta = a + b/r^3. The crossed-out lines 'epsilon = {..} + {..}/r^3' and 'delta = {..} + {9.6360613}/r^3' are of this type. The next page solves the resulting equation with the auxiliary angle H.
- I cannot reconstruct every number in these columns, e.g. 8.4495692 or 9.1492769. They end in log Sigma = 8.3992165/8.3992169, i.e. a division by Sigma.
- Bottom-right products are prepared for formulas 2/-3/ of folio 61:
  - D'' sin(V''-V) = 9.5491443;
  - D sin(V''-V) = 9.5506347;
  - D' sin(V''-V') = 9.0735178;
  - D' sin(V'-V) = 9.3826449.

(4) DIFFERENTIAL TRANSFORMATION ('Die Differenzialänderungen der Länge und Breite durch die der Rect. u. Decl. ausgedr.'). Consider the spherical triangle formed by the equator pole, the ecliptic pole and the star. Its sides are eps, 90°-delta and 90°-beta. Let P be the angle at the star.
- By the sine rule, sin P = sin eps cos lambda / cos delta = sin eps cos alpha / cos beta (here alpha = right ascension).
- By the cosine rule, cos P = (cos eps - sin beta sin delta)/(cos beta cos delta). So P > 90° exactly when cos eps < sin beta sin delta.
- Then cos beta d lambda = cos P cos delta d alpha + sin P d delta, i.e. d lambda = (cos P cos delta/cos beta) d alpha + (sin P/cos beta) d delta.
- And d beta = -sin P cos delta d alpha + cos P d delta.

Beispiel I. Inputs: log sin eps = 9.60010, log cos alpha = 9.98742, log cos beta = 9.93846, log cos lambda = 9.94266, log cos delta = 9.89370. The step that check (9.60010+9.94266-9.89370 = 9.64906) is mine.
- log sin P = 9.60010 + 0.04896 = 9.64906. The same value follows from the other expression.
- log cos P = 9.95191 (P ≈ 26°28').
- Coefficients: log(cos P cos delta/cos beta) = 9.90715, log(sin P/cos beta) = 9.71060, log(sin P cos delta) = 9.54276n, log cos P = 9.95191.
- With d alpha = +2.5" (log 0.39794) and d delta = +6" (log 0.77815): d lambda = 2.019 + 3.081 = +5.10", d beta = -0.872 + 5.371 = +4.50".

Beispiel II (second star). d alpha = +6 1/3" (log 0.80163), d delta = +1 2/3" (log 0.22185). Coefficients are 9.94825, 9.63863, 9.58742n, 9.95890. Result: d lambda = 5.622 + 0.725 = +6.35", d beta = -2.449 + 1.516 = -0.93".

Beispiel III (third star). d alpha = -0.97" (log 9.98677n, written '-1"'), d delta = +21.96" (log 1.34163, written '+22"'). Coefficients are 9.94437, 9.64516, 9.58300n, 9.95833. Result: d lambda = -0.853 + 9.700 = +8.85", d beta = 0.371 + 19.951 = +20.32".

(5) APPLYING THE CORRECTIONS. These d lambda are added to the original longitudes:
- 28°47'58.29" + 5.10" = 28°48'3.39";
- 13°46'22.16" + 6.35" = 13°46'28.51";
- 344°1'41.14" + 8.85" = 344°1'49.99".
The corrected latitudes are 29°47'11.06", 17°22'5.15" and (south) 18°53'36.21". Their log tangents, 9.7576923, 9.4952246, 9.5343405n, feed the recomputation of Sigma and A, A', A'' in (2)-(3). The page is thus a full reduction of three observations (RA/Dec corrections converted to ecliptic) followed by the constants of Gauss's 1805 three-observation equation.
errors: In the left column of the Sigma sum, '+0,08882102' must be 0.08872102: the sum shown, 0.30902366, and the true product 10^(8.9482311-10) = 0.088763 both require it. Either a slip or a misreading. The recomputed column (8876281) is right.
The labels 'd alpha = -1"', 'd delta = +22"' in example III and '+1 1/3' in example II are only nominal. The logarithms actually used correspond to -0.97", +21.96" and +1 2/3" (log 5/3 = 0.22185).

The P>90° criterion as transcribed reads 'cos eps > sin beta sin delta'. From cos P = (cos eps - sin beta sin delta)/(cos beta cos delta) the correct condition is cos eps < sin beta sin delta. Either Gauss's inequality sign is reversed or this is a transcription problem.
Two successive values of log Sigma (8.3982597, then 8.3992165) are superseded by 8.3984242 after the positions were corrected. These are revisions, not errors in the final value.

Apart from these, every check I made of the logarithmic arithmetic agrees to the last unit or two. That covers sin P/cos P consistency, the four coefficients in each example, the products, Sigma, the A-values and the weights summing to 1.

results.what: Conversion of small corrections in right ascension/declination into corrections of ecliptic longitude/latitude via the position angle P between the hour circle and the circle of latitude: sin P = sin eps cos lambda/cos delta = sin eps cos alpha/cos beta; cos beta d lambda = cos P cos delta d alpha + sin P d delta; d beta = -sin P cos delta d alpha + cos P d delta
results.modern_name: Differential relations between equatorial and ecliptic coordinates (angle between the two pole directions, 'parallactic angle' of the ecliptic)

results.what: Numerical example of the three-observation determinant Sigma = theta sin(alpha''-alpha') - theta' sin(alpha''-alpha) + theta'' sin(alpha'-alpha), together with A, A', A'' and time-interpolation weights, leading to a relation delta = a + b/r^3 for the geocentric distance
results.modern_name: Lagrange-Laplace-Gauss fundamental equation of preliminary orbit determination (geocentric distance as a function of 1/r^3)

results.what: Approximation of the triangle ratio by the time ratio with correction factor 1 + M(V'-V)(V''-V')/(2r'^3), first hypothesis k/k''=1, M=1
results.modern_name: Series approximation of the triangle-area ratios (Gauss's n/n'' ≈ tau/tau'' (1 + ...))

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine working page: a reduction example and standard differential formulas. It is a working example of Gauss's known 1805 orbit-determination machinery, probably applied to the 1805 comet. There is nothing beyond what is known from his methods and published work.
